results.summary: This design is a power supply sequencer that enables and disables eight output channels in a controlled order with a configurable delay. It uses counters and registers to track channel states, with the delay set via a 5-bit input. To test, apply a clock and reset, then toggle the enable input to sequence channels on and off. It requires no external hardware but is intended for applications like GaAs amplifiers needing sequenced power supplies.

This is a simple UART transmitter module that sends 8-bit data at 115200 baud. To use it, present the data on the parallel input pins and assert the send pin; the module then transmits the data serially on the TX pin. It requires only a clock input and no external hardware beyond a UART receiver. The design is straightforward and suitable for basic serial communication tasks.

The documentation for this project is minimal, providing only a title and a single pin description for duty cycle input. It appears to be a PWM generator, but the details of operation, testing, and external hardware requirements are not described. The summary is based on the title and pin name, with limited confidence.

This is a PWM generator with duty cycle control via a 7-bit input. An internal counter increments each clock cycle and is compared against the duty cycle value to produce the PWM output. To use it, provide a clock and set the duty cycle input to the desired percentage. It requires no external hardware beyond a clock source and output monitoring.

This design plays the Super Mario tune over a piezo speaker connected across two output pins. It uses a 100 kHz clock and a reset input to start the playback. The output is a differential sound wave, so a piezo speaker should be connected across the two pins. It is a music player example demonstrating PWM-based sound generation.

This is a Verilog implementation of the classic AY-3-8913 programmable sound generator, featuring three tone channels, a noise generator, and an envelope generator. It provides both digital 8-bit audio output and PWM outputs for external DAC or filtering. The chip is programmed via a multiplexed data/address bus with control pins, and it has been silicon-tested with a framework that reads YM files. It is notable for its fidelity to the original chip and its compact single-tile implementation.

This is a digital PWM generator with selectable resolution (5 to 9 bits), dyadic modulation, and dithering. It provides complementary high-side and low-side outputs with dead-time, suitable for power electronics like synchronous buck converters. Configuration is done via a register file written through the pins, and it defaults to 8-bit normal PWM. The cocotb testbench exercises reset, widths, and dead-time, and no external hardware is required for bench testing.

This is a spiking neural network (SNN) with reward-based learning using STDP. It consists of 8 layers, each with 2 neurons, and weights are loaded from memory via a 4-bit input with address lines. The design is intended for machine learning experiments, but the documentation is sparse on testing and external hardware. It likely requires a controller to load weights and provide inputs.

This is an AXI-Stream Matrix Vector Multiplier with a UART interface. It requires an external USB-FTDI adapter for UART communication to load data and retrieve results. The design performs matrix-vector multiplication, likely for DSP or machine learning applications. It is notable for its streaming interface and compact implementation.

This is an 8-bit minimal CPU with 8 registers, an ALU, branches, and a JAL instruction. It is programmed by feeding 16-bit instructions in two cycles via the input pins, with control signals on the bidirectional pins. The program counter is output, allowing an external ROM to supply instructions. It requires no external hardware beyond the ROM and is driven entirely through the pins.
